ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M1.-Key-C.title: M1. Key Concepts And Terminology
ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M1.-Key-C.content:
Overall Definitions

Health inequality: measurable difference in health between social groups.
Health inequity: preventable and unfair differences in health/well-being/access to quality health services across individuals/population subgroups/countries. It arises from the unequal and unfair distribution of power/wealth/other social resources.
Health equity: the absence of unfair, avoidable differences in health among population groups.
Monitoring is the process of repeatedly making observations of a situation to watch for changes over time

Generally, the goal of HIM is to inform implementation of changes to advance health equity and improve health of disadvantaged populations.



There are two essential measurement to health inequality monitoring: (1) health indicators & (2)dimensions of inequality (demographic, socioeconomic, geographical criteria )
1) Health Indicators
Health can be measured at different levels of the health sector. The WHO Monitoring, evaluation and review framework categorizes health indicators into four components:

2) Dimensions of Inequality
Dimensions of inequality: criteria used to define subgroups within a population. Subgroups are used for comparison in health inequality analysis.
Data specific to population subgroups is known as disaggregated data.
Related concepts to HIM
Concept 1. Human rights & HIM:

Human rights are moral aspirations based on the inherent dignity and equality of the human person expressed in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
A human rights-based approach specifically aims to realize human rights, including the right to health. HIM should consider how human rights are protected, promoted, enforced or violated.

Concept 2. Gender:
Gender refers to the socially constructed norms, roles, behaviours, and relations among and between women, men, girls, boys, and gender diverse people. Gender norms, roles, and relations influence individual identity, interpersonal relationships, and institutional structures and institutions.
Concept 3. Social determinants of health (SDH):
SDH are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems shaping the conditions of daily life that impact health.
Many social determinants of health operate across multiple sectors of society.

Multisectoral actions for health are those actions undertaken in non-health sectors  to promote healthy populations.

Concept 4. Primary health care(PHC)
PHC is founded on the idea that all people deserve the right care, right in their community. One of the goals of HIM is to contribute to strengthening PHC. SDGs30 rely on the principle of Leaving No One Behind (equity values), which is aligned with PHC goals.
Components  & approaches of PHC

addresses health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care (⇒ holistic approach).
seeks impact as close as feasible to people’s everyday environments and takes into account people needs and preferences as individuals (⇒ person-centered approach) and communities (⇒ whole-of-society approach) .

Specific goals of PHC:
• addressing the broader determinants of health through multisectoral policy and action
• empowering individuals, families and communities to take charge of their own health.
• meeting the majority of people’s health needs throughout their lives;

Concept 5. Progressive realization of universal health coverage:
Make decisions to expand coverage of health services, extending those services to non-covered population and, as part of financial protection, reducing costs.

ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M2.-Situa.title: M2. Situating HIM
ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M2.-Situa.content:
During the beginning stages, it is important to think deeply about the overarching purpose of the specific monitoring activity. This, in turn, will guide subsequent planning about the specifics of how monitoring will be conducted.
Below are some guiding questions to prepare HIM:

Why is health inequality monitoring being done at this time?
What is the intended impact of monitoring?
Which policy cycles or windows of opportunity are important to keep in mind?
How often should health inequality monitoring be done?
Which groups of people will use the knowledge generated from the monitoring exercise?
How can the interests and needs of affected populations be understood and represented?
What are the data requirements for monitoring?

Overall, the goals of these questions are to discuss the importance and purpose of health inequality monitoring, and describe who is involved, when it should be done, and how it is aligned within health information systems and other health sector activities.

ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M3.-Cycle.title: M3. Cycle of monitoring
ELearningCourses/1.Foundations/M3.-Cycle.content:
Five steps in HIM.  It is a cyclic and iterative process.

Below some detailed guidelines for each step.

ELearningCourses/2.Data-Sources/0.-Intro.title: 0. Intro
ELearningCourses/2.Data-Sources/0.-Intro.content:
Goals of this course section:

Describe the attributes of high-quality data sources for health inequality monitoring;
Describe general categories of data sources;

High-quality data sources share a number of general attributes. They contain data that are timely, complete, accurate, reliable and accessible.
The SCORE for Health Data Technical Package (by WHO and partners) aims to improve the quality, availability, accessibility and analysis of data in countries. Global reports and dashboards provide insights into the strength of data sources in countries.
There are two main categories of data sources that are relevant to health inequality monitoring: (1)population-based sources and (2)institution-based sources.


Population-based sources contain information on every individual in a population or a representative sample of a population. Examples of population-based sources include household surveys, civil registration and vital statistics systems, and censuses.


Institution-based sources collect information in the course of administrative and operational activities. Examples of administrative data include records kept by health facilities or by other institutions outside of the health sector.


Other data sources:
3) Surveillance systems often combine population-based and institution-based data.
4) Health facility surveys
Health facility surveys collect information such as the availability of services in facilities and the capacities of facilities to deliver quality services. Data are collected on an intermittent basis by external teams of data collectors. Examples of surveys include:
WHO Harmonized Health Facility Assessment (HHFA), the WHO Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA), the USAID Service Provision Assessment (SPA) and the World Bank Service Delivery Indicators (SDI) surveys.
Data that are modelled or triangulated from multiple sources may also be used for health inequality monitoring in the absence of reliable direct measures.

ELearningCourses/2.Data-Sources/M.Descri.title: M.Description of all modules
ELearningCourses/2.Data-Sources/M.Descri.content:
The modules described in this course are the following:

M1. Household Surveys
M2. Administrative Data Sources
M3. Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Systems
M4. Censuses
M5. Data Source Mapping
M6. Data Linking

Modules 1-4
The following table describes contents in modules 1-4: HIMFoundations2DataSources_NotesSummary.xlsx
Modules 5-6
Some words about topics in module 5 to 6.
M5. Data sourcing:
The main goal of data source mapping is to determine where data for health inequality monitoring can be sourced. Data source mapping creates an inventory of available data sources that contain information about health indicators and dimensions of inequality – and then facilitates cross-referencing between sources.
Data source mapping can be broken down into four sequential tables, each building on the previous.

Table 1: Creating a list of available data sources, specifying the source type (census, administrative source, household survey, CRVS, etc.), the name of the source, and the year (or years) of data collection.
Table 2: An expanded version of the first, focusing on dimensions of inequality.
Table 3: table compiles the health indicator data contained within each data source
Table 4: Integrates the information from the second and third tables, indicating the data sources that contain both health indicator and dimension of inequality data.
Online templates for these four tables are available.
As a follow up from data source mapping, the strengths and limitations of different data sources should be weighed,

M6. Data Linking:
Data linking involves merging information about health indicators and dimensions of inequality from different data sources using a common identifier.
Building on the data source mapping exercise outlined in Module 5, an additional fifth table can be created to assess the possibility of data linking.
It is important to adhere to data protection protocols to ensure that confidentiality is maintained.
If HIM cannot proceed as planned (lack of data), the focus of monitoring may need to be adjusted.

ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.filePath: ELearningCourses/3.Health Disaggregation/M1. Health Indicators and dimensions of inequality.md
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.title: M1. Health Indicators and dimensions of inequality
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.content:
Health indicators
An indicator is a measurement that reflects a given situation. For our purposes, it is a quantitative metric that is used to monitor performance (:measure results against targets) and assess accountability.
Selection of health indicator could be narrowly or broadly defined. Examples:

Narrowly defined i.e:  reflect the coverage of an intervention and associated  outcomes and impacts.
Broadly defined i.e: show health service access across the continuum of care for a particular condition.

The WHO Monitoring, Evaluation and Review Framework organizes health indicators according to four indicator domains: (1) Inputs and processes, (2) Outputs, (3) Outcome , (4) Impact indicators.

Tracer & Composite indicators
Tracer indicators are specific indicators that stand in for a broader health topic. Tracer indicators are straightforward to understand and report, although they may not be representative of the processes involving the broader topic.
Composite indicators combine multiple indicators, sometimes across different health topics, into an index, thus generating an overall picture of the health topic.
Example of tracer & composite indicators
Indicators to monitor reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health:

Another example of complex indicator, the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Service Coverage Index:

The UHC service coverage index is measured as a unitless score between 0 and 100, where lower scores indicate lower average coverage of essential health services.
Using an indicator with a standardized definition can facilitate benchmarking, as other populations may have comparable data about the indicator.  WHO Global Reference List contains a standard list of 100 core health indicators, plus indicators for the health-related Sustainable Development Goals.
Measuring health indicators
Health indicators are generally measured as absolute counts or relative terms (such as proportions or rates). Indicators measured in relative terms are constructed as a numerator and denominator. For a proportion, the numerator is a subset of the denominator. For example, the percentage of births attended by skilled health personnel is the number of births attended by skilled health personnel (numerator), divided by the total number of live births (denominator).
Dimensions of inequality
Dimensions of inequality are the criteria used to define population subgroups that serve as the basis of comparison for health inequality analyses.
Certain inequality dimensions have common applicability and data availability across most settings and topics. As well, context-specific dimensions of inequality are numerous and varied, including caste or tribe, criminal status, indigenous status, language spoken at home etc…
Considerations when selecting dimensions of inequality

Certain dimensions may not be applicable (Disaggregating the use of maternal health services by the sex of the individual or sex of the child, for instance, does not make sense.).
Selection of dimensions of inequality should involve consultation with relevant stakeholders.

Single dimensions or multiple dimensions more adapted?


Intersectionality – defined as the coexistence of multiple characteristics and identities that together compound disadvantage due to the interactions among them – may warrant consideration

Double (applying two dimensions of inequality) or multiple disaggregation is a starting point of exploring intersectionality through health inequality monitoring.

ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.filePath: ELearningCourses/3.Health Disaggregation/M3. Categorizing dimensions of inequality.md
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.title: M3. Categorizing dimensions of inequality
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.content:
Categorizing dimensions of inequality
The subgroup composition describes which individuals are grouped together based on their profiles.  There are several factors to take into consideration when deciding the best option for categorizing subgroups.
Consideration 1: Granularity
Granularity of the available information. More granular (:more detailed) information allows for a greater range of options for categorizing subgroups.
Consideration 2: Sample Size
Consequences of having a small sample size:

resulting estimate is not reliable.
further analysis is limited.
In some cases, may pose a risk to confidentiality. Individual with unique or rare characteristics may be identifiable.

Addressing a small sample size:

Calculating the standard error or confidence intervals are helpful reliability of estimates.
The Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) requires to flag estimates from sample sizes ranging between 25-49 individuals.
Drop estimate
Recategorizing the inequality dimension by combining data from multiple responses that consequently has a larger sample size.

Consideration 3: Resolution issue
Generally, a smaller number of subgroups for a dimension of inequality will capture less heterogeneity (or variation) between the subgroups.
Below the amplitude of inequality by wealth is larger by wealth deciles than by wealth quintiles. This example drives interest to choosing the appropriate and useful segmentation of variables.

ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.filePath: ELearningCourses/3.Health Disaggregation/M4. Reporting disaggregated health data.md
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.title: M4. Reporting disaggregated health data
ELearningCourses/3.Health-Disaggregation.content:
Best practices & advantages of disaggregated data
The interpretation of disaggregated data tends to be intuitive, therefore they are appropriate for most audiences. In some cases, the main conclusions from the data can be adequately supported using disaggregated data, without the need for other technical content such as summary measures of health inequality.

Disaggregated data should be reported alongside other pertinent information (overall average, sample sizes, uncertainty measures) to situate the results.  Explaining why monitoring was undertaken, in other words, providing context, is important.
Describing patterns in disaggregated data can be a compelling way to assess and report disaggregated health data for dimensions of inequality that are ordered, such as age, economic status or education

Example of patterns
Example of inequality pattern are represented by the graphs below.


Complete coverage: green line


Pattern of marginal exclusion, purple line. The poorest quintile has much lower coverage than the four richer quintiles.


Queuing or linear pattern, blue line. There are increases in coverage across each of the quintiles.
- Intervention: A combination approach, with differentiated targeting across the population subgroups is warranted.


Mass deprivation pattern,red line, most of the population – all but the richest in quintile 5 – has low levels of coverage.
-Intervention: population-level response may be required to reach all (or most) of the population






These four patterns can also be displayed using Equiplots. Here, the health indicator is on the bottom axis, and the subgroups are represented by coloured circles.

In Jordan, has a pattern of universal coverage. Health coverage across all population subgroups is high.
Approaches to report disaggregated data
Table with visual features
A table facilitates quick interpretation of the data if it contains only key information. It can be useful to use colour coding and round to the neared whole number.

ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.filePath: ELearningCourses/4. Summary Measure of Health Inequality/M1. Defining characteristics of summary measures.md
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.title: M1. Defining characteristics of summary measures
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.content:
Simple VS Complex summary measures
Simple measures
Simple measures make pairwise comparisons between two subgroups. They are especially relevant for dimensions of inequality that are binary.

Comparisons can be made between any two subgroups that are of special interest. In some cases, it may be appropriate to calculate pairwise measures multiple times for different combinations of subgroups.
The two most basic simple measures of inequality are difference and ratio.

Complex measures
Two major types of complex measures: ordered dimensions of inequality VS non-ordered dimensions of inequality.

Ordered dimensions of inequality have an inherent positioning and can be ranked.
Non-ordered dimensions of inequality are based on criteria that cannot be logically ranked, such as subnational regions, languages spoken, race or ethnicity.

Ordered and non-ordered complex summary measures can be further described as weighted or unweighted.

Weighted measures take into account the population size of each subgroup
Unweighted measures treat each subgroup as equally sized.

While complex measures may be weighted or unweighted, simple measures are always unweighted.
Some complex measures of inequality require the use of a reference point, which serves as a benchmark or point of comparison.
Reference points that are subgroups: subgroup at the extreme, subgroup with special significance, best-performing subgroup.
Other reference points: overall average of the health indicator, health indicator target.

Absolute VS Relative inequality measures
Simple and complex summary measures of health inequality can be broadly divided into absolute inequality measures and relative inequality measures. Absolute and relative measures of inequality provide complementary perspectives to assess a situation of inequality. Therefore, they should be both calculated and taken into account when interpreting findings.

ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.filePath: ELearningCourses/4. Summary Measure of Health Inequality/M2. Simple Summary Measures.md
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.title: M2. Simple Summary Measures
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.content:
Favorable and adverse health indicators
There are favorable and adverse health indicators.  Certain indicators, however, present a more nuanced situation, where the health indicator is not obviously favourable or adverse. The desired situation is neither the maximum nor the minimum.
Difference and ratio
Difference
They make pairwise comparisons. In cases where there are more than two subgroups, we can use data from two selected subgroups.

For favourable health indicators, the difference is calculated as the advantaged subgroup estimate minus the disadvantaged subgroup estimate.
For adverse health indicators, the difference is calculated as the disadvantaged subgroup estimate minus the advantaged subgroup estimate.

For non-ordered dimensions consisting of more than two subgroups, difference is usually calculated as the highest minus the lowest subgroup estimate, regardless of the indicator type.
Ratio
Ratio is a measure of relative inequality. It is multiplicative, showing how much better (or worse) one subgroup is doing in relation to the other. Ratio values are unitless.

ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.filePath: ELearningCourses/4. Summary Measure of Health Inequality/M3. Complex Summary Measures.md
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.title: M3. Complex Summary Measures
ELearningCourses/4.-Summary-Measure-of-H.content:
Complex summary measures of health inequality are calculated using information about all subgroups of a population. They are appropriate to use with dimensions of inequality comprised of more than two subgroups.  This decision chart can be used as a quick guide for determining which common complex summary measures of health inequality are appropriate for use in different applications.

Some complex summary measures
Mean difference from best group expresses the absolute mean difference between each subgroup and the reference subgroup with the most favourable estimate.
Population attributable risk: the absolute improvement in a setting average (such as national average) that could be achieved if all population subgroups had the same level of health as a reference point.
Here is a graphical representation of PAR:

Population attributable fraction: Expresses the same information as PAR in relative terms. Calculated by dividing PAR by setting average and multiplying by 100.
HEAT & HEAT Plus
Key tools that aid with calculation of complex summary measures are integrated in the WHO Health Equity Assessment Toolkit.

HEAT, Built-in Database Edition: comes with preinstalled datasets consisting of all disaggregated data in the WHO Health Inequality Data Repository
HEAT Plus: enables users to upload and work with their own database

ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/0.Intro.title: 0.Intro
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/0.Intro.content:
Reporting may be a precursor or may be embedded in knowledge translation activities. Reporting will reflect aspects of all the previous steps of the inequality monitoring cycle: (1) overarching purpose and scope of monitoring, (2)data sources, (3)key results.
At this stage, a special focus given to:

contextualize findings

Information about context, affected populations and findings from qualitative sources, if available, should be integrated.


data and results curation and interpreted.

Importantly, reporting should not contribute to stigma or discrimination against population groups.
Reporting formats:

Written reports
Academic publications
Policy briefs
Interactive displays
Presentation such as webinars, interviews and conferences

In the following doc, we describe reporting format and their adapted audience: ReportingTypes.xlsx

ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M1.-Purpos.title: M1. Purpose and Audience
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M1.-Purpos.content:
Purpose
The general purpose of reporting is to raise awareness and share knowledge.
To convey why reporting is being done it is important to share what the aims, goals and objectives are. All aspects of reporting should be aligned with the purpose. For outputs and results to be impactful, they reflect relevance with the purpose.
An example of how aims, goals and objective are aligned with the purpose in a schematic representation:

Purpose driven reporting ensures all aspects of reporting align with the stated purpose, including identifying an appropriate audience.  Members of the target audience should be consulted in the development of reporting outputs.
Purpose describes: why reporting is being done
Goal describes: specific outcome of reporting
Objective describes: actions to achieve reporting goals
Aim describes: the ideal that underlie reporting
Audience
Audience should be positioned to support the intended outcome of reporting. Reporting outputs should be developed in consideration of the audience (prior knowledge, skills, needs, interests).

Does the audience have a predefined interest in the topic area?

Can the audience help achieve goals and objectives of reporting?



The audience may be quite targeted (ministry of health) or may encompass diverse groups of people (researchers, community leader, policy-makers, knowledge users).
Understanding the audience:

Be familiar with the interests, needs and preferences of the target audience

Ensure that reporting is relevant and accessible.



Type of reporting depending on the audience interests, needs and preferences:

Researchers and scientists: detailed technical contents
Policy makers or programme managers: succinct summaries with clear and timely recommendations
General audiences: plain language, focusing on new and relatable insights

In depth understanding may require seeking to know the audience’s:

Prevailing biases or misconceptions
Ways of accessing information
Technical ability
Type of language (technical or plain) and level
Level of digital literacy
Relevant political, cultural and social influences
Process for using and sharing info
Potential sensitivities

Member of the target should be involved in the development of reporting, outputs and approaches.

ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M2.-Scope-.filePath: ELearningCourses/5. Reporting/M2. Scope and Technical Content.md
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M2.-Scope-.title: M2. Scope and Technical Content
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M2.-Scope-.content:
Scope
The scope generally refers to:

The latest status reported

Reporting the latest status of inequality is important.


Change over time

Compares the latest status from data from previous period(s).
Is the situation improving? Staying the same?


Benchmarking

Compares the level of inequality across similar settings (i.e: economic related inequality across countries/across provinces  )
Requires that the data are reasonably comparable (i.e: collected in the same time period, using similar methods)



Technical Content
Specific results that support finding and conclusions:

Disaggregated data
Summary measures
Technical details
Information about metadata and methods

Technical content needs to be selected depending on the audience. It needs to always be transparent, accurate and easy to understand for the audience.
The technical content presented depends on the reporting format chosen:

Journal articles focus on detailed methods and results
Policy-briefs have a greater focus on the applications and use of findings.

When selecting technical content, disaggregated data is a good starting point because:

Pattern description across population are straightforward/intuitive and therefore appropriate for diverse audiences.

Summary measures should only be presented if they enhance the impact of reporting. Some of the advantages of summary measures are:

a single number to describe inequality
quick for comparisons
Generally, it is good to accompany summary measures with disaggregated data.

A reminder of what simple and complex summary measures are:

Other key elements to contextualize findings :

Overage average of the health indicator
population size: number of affected people in each subgroup
population share of those affected
uncertainty measures

Importantly, health inequality reporting should focus on relevant data rather than including all available information.

ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M3.-Data-P.title: M3. Data Presentation Approaches
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M3.-Data-P.content:
Text:
Effective to explain complicated findings or nuanced conclusions and describe their significance. Ideally, text is descriptive and concise and adapted to a lower reading level to that of the audience. Text should be formatted in a logical way.
Tables:
Can be used to present data concisely. Look up for particular values. But require further effort from the audience than graphs. Useful if precision required. Should have descriptive titles and headers to render the table easy to read. Same level of precision of value should given to all number (same position of decimal points).
Graphs:
Make patterns and outliers visible. Support rapid comparisons across values. How to select appropriate types of graphs depending on the case is important. In the additional ressources of this course, some readings provide recommendations on the graph types and applicabilities/adaptability.
It is generally preferable to adopt a few types of graphs. It is best to use the most ideal type of graph and continue to present throughout the report where needed. This approach helps with consistency and accessibility of the report.
Recommendations:

Do not use too many features
Each feature should highlight a key element of the take-away messages
Include explanatory text where needed

Maps
Impactful with all types of audiences. Generally display one variable at a time and often use thresholds to colour areas.
Considerations:

Note where data is not available and contested border areas.
Comparing between maps is not recommended as it is a tedious exercise.

Interactive data visuals
Present large amount of data in an approachable and modifiable format. Make it possible to drill through various levels of data to create a narrow view focus. The use of interactive data visuals requires the audience to have digital literacy and access. For more info on best practices to develop interactive visual, can check the additional ressources of this module.
A piece of advise:
There are advantages to applying different presentation approaches. To best exploit a combination of approaches, we must ensure that they complement each other, rather than repeating key messages in different formats.

ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M4.-Best-P.title: M4. Best Practices
ELearningCourses/5.-Reporting/M4.-Best-P.content:
Useful take-aways of this module:

Discuss consideration for reporting background and methods
Refer to a checklist to ensure that reporting outputs contain the necessary details
Access examles of effective written reports
Piece of advice: Maintaining detailed notes across all steps may make reporting easier.

Background and context
Background and context situates the purpose of monitoring. Questions such as:

Why was monitoring undertaken?
What is monitoring setting out to accomplish?

Methods
Discussing methods and approaches is important to understand how the data supports or does not support certain conclusions. In this step, the parameters, their limitations, suitability, and excluded alternatives are described. (The depth and level of detail depends on the audience.). In journal article the level of detail needs to be sufficient such that the presented analysis could be replicated by third-parties.
Findings and conclusions
Generally results are presented going from a wide scope into a narrower focus. Findings should be complemented by implications.
Best practices:


When simple and complex summary measures support the same conclusion, it is preferable to just report the simple summary measures. When there are discrepancies, complex measures can be presented if the audience has technical knowledge, otherwise, explaining the reason of the discrepancy is recommended.


Both absolute and relative summary measures, overall average and disagregated data should be reported.


Reporting population share is important, especially if the size of subgroups are varied.


Report national avrages alongside disaggregated data


Consider whether reporting statistical significance is appropriate (shows a difference that is meaningful from a public health perspective). /!\ : careful with small differences that have statistical significance because they are based of large sample sizes. Careful with making false conclusions that are produced from statistical constructs.

Ressources/00.-Ressource-List.title: 00. Ressource List
Ressources/00.-Ressource-List.content:
WHO has developed numerous resources to support health inequality monitoring, which are all accessible through the Health Inequality Monitor website. We will detail some of these ressources in this section.
Skill building ressources
There are various E-Learning courses that help build quantitative analysis skills.
Some courses teach how to conduct data disaggregation depending on the software:

Stata
[R software](thegraphcourses.org/courses/inequality-analysis-using-r-disaggregated-data-from-surveys/](thegraphcourses.org/courses/inequality-analysis-using-r-disaggregated-data-from-surveys/)
Excel

There is a course on how to use the Health Equity Assessment Toolkit (HEAT and HEAT Plus) developed by WHO: course .
HEAT and HEAT Plus are interactive applications that allow users to explore patterns of inequality in the WHO health inequality data repository. Sources of data included are household surveys such as, DHS and MICS, or other external sources such as Eurodata. Heat and Heat Plus can interactively disaggregate data, calculate summary measures of inequality, compare inequality between settings, and create and export customized results.
HEAT can be explored here: link.
Youtube tutorial on how to navigate around HEAT:link
Hanbooks, manuals, reports


Book, Harnessing data to advance health equity, link.
This is a book that compiles detailed information on health inequality monitoring. Part 2 in this book, Generating Impact, is not directly covered in the E-Learning course. Part 4, Analysis and Reporting, discusses many technical elements and calculating measures and interpreting data. This chapter may be worth reviewing indefinite times.


Manual, a step-by-step manual to National Health Inequality Monitoring: link.
This manual describes the steps to monitoring that are described in the E-Learning Courses. The structure is the same. It is an interesting source if we want to delve into some detail on the sections.

Childhood Immunization: Exploring Inequalities with Childhood Immunization data
